# Diagnosing the "Coughing" AC Compressor on a 2002 Subaru Impreza

You started with a classic symptom: the compressor engages, but the system is empty or nearly so. You recharged it, and for three minutes, you got cold air. That initial burst of cooling proves the compressor clutch has power and the high-side pressure sensor isn't immediately shutting it down on startup. However, the subsequent behaviorâhot air followed by a rhythmic "coughing" every four seconds that stalling your engine speedâis a specific diagnostic signature. It indicates the compressor is attempting to engage or cycle rapidly while a safety mechanism aborts the operation, causing a load spike that momentarily drops RPM.

The core issue here is almost certainly low refrigerant pressure triggering the Low-Pressure Cut-Out switch. In a properly charged system, the evaporator maintains a specific saturation temperature. When refrigerant levels drop significantly, the evaporator coils become too cold for the air volume passing through them, causing moisture to freeze into ice. This ice buildup restricts airflow and physically blocks the suction line.

Your observation that the pressure gauge read near zero before and after the recharge confirms the system is not holding charge. You added an 18 oz can, which likely wasn't enough to fill the volume if there was a leak, or the refrigerant boiled off immediately due to the heat soak from the engine bay. The fact that you still got cold air initially suggests the new refrigerant pushed the pressure up just enough to melt the existing ice temporarily, allowing the compressor to run until it hit its low-pressure threshold again.

The "coughing" every four seconds is likely a result of the compressor clutch cycling erratically. Many AC systems have a pressure switch that disengages the clutch if the high-side pressure gets too high or the low-side pressure gets too low. If your system has a super-slow leak, you are constantly in this starvation mode where the compressor tries to work but can't maintain pressure. The hiccup in engine speed happens because the A/C compressor acts as a parasitic load; when the clutch engages under these abnormal conditions, the sudden torque demand causes the RPM to dip noticeably, especially at lower speeds or during acceleration.

### Troubleshooting Steps Before Professional Service

Before spending hundreds of dollars on repairs, you can perform a few targeted checks using basic tools available at an auto parts store.

First, verify the current refrigerant pressure without adding more charge yet. Connect a manifold gauge set to the low-pressure service port. Start the engine and turn the AC to maximum cold. If the low-side pressure remains near 0 PSI, you have a confirmed leak. The system cannot be recharged effectively until the breach is sealed, because any gas added will simply escape as fast as it enters.

Second, inspect the evaporator for ice. Since the car has been sitting with low charge, there may still be ice on the evaporator core inside the dashboard. Running the AC in "defrost" mode or slightly opening the recirculation door can sometimes help melt residual ice without overloading the system immediately. However, if the pressure is zero, this will only provide temporary relief.

### The Leak Detection Reality

The decision to add more refrigerant is a trade-off between cost and efficacy. Adding more R-134a without fixing the leak is like putting a bandage on a punctured tire while driving at high speed. It works for a short distance, then fails catastrophically. Given that your 2002 Subaru Impreza has gone 12 years with a slow leak, it is highly probable that there is a significant breach somewhere in the lines, condenser, or O-rings.

If you choose to recharge again, do so only after ensuring the system is clean and free of air. Using an oil can to charge blindly often introduces non-condensables, which raise operating temperatures and reduce cooling efficiency further. If the pressure still reads near zero after a proper recharge attempt, the leak rate is faster than the recharge rate.

At this point, you have two viable paths. You can continue DIY troubleshooting by inspecting visible lines for damage or testing the compressor clutch coil resistance with a multimeter to ensure it's not failing electrically. Alternatively, taking the vehicle to a mechanic for a UV dye leak detection or electronic nitrogen leak test is often more cost-effective in the long run if the repair involves replacing major components like the condenser or evaporator.

If you decide to seek professional help, ensure the shop performs a pressure hold test after recharging. If the pressure drops over an hour, the leak has not been located and sealed. For complex electrical issues where the compressor itself is failing due to internal damage from low-pressure operation, replacement might be necessary regardless of the refrigerant charge level.
